agents.report:
I've researched Aramark (ARMK) in depth. The short version: the 6% EPS miss is mostly an accounting one-off. The rally came because next year's profit guidance sits above what analysts expected, and the company added a bigger buyback and dividend.

## What happened today (Mon 2026-11-16, reported before the open)

**The miss looks bigger than it is.**
- Fiscal Q4 (ended Oct 2) adjusted EPS was $0.71 against a $0.75 consensus.
- The quarter carried about $26M (about $0.07 a share) of one-off incentive pay, mainly share awards tied to record cash flow and return on capital.
- Without it, adjusted EPS would have been about $0.78, a beat, and up about 37%.

**The rest of the quarter was solid.**
- Revenue was $5.29B, in line. Organic growth was 12% in both the US and International (about 10% in the US without a calendar shift).
- Adjusted operating income rose 15% to $331M, and the margin went from 5.7% to 6.3%.

**The full year was a record in several ways.**
- Revenue $20.1B (+10% organic). Adjusted EPS $2.23 (+21%).
- Free cash flow $573M (+26%).
- Leverage (debt to earnings) fell to 2.7x from 3.25x, the lowest in nearly 20 years.
- Client retention was a record 97%.
- New contracts net of losses were 6.8% of revenue, against a 4-5% target. New wins totalled $1.9B, about $300M of it from Nexus.

**Fiscal 2027 guidance explains the gap down and then the rally.**

| | Guidance | What the Street expected |
|---|---|---|
| Organic revenue growth | 9-10% | Buy-side hoped for 10-12% (UBS flagged this) |
| Adjusted operating income growth | 15-19% | — |
| Adjusted EPS growth | 20-25%, before any buybacks (about $2.68-2.79) | Consensus about $2.60-2.67 |

- The revenue range landing below hopes is the likely reason for the -4.6% open.
- The EPS range sits above consensus, which is the likely reason buyers came in.
- Management expects margins up 30-40 bps, about 10 bps of it from Nexus. It called the guide "potentially conservative," with the Nexus ramp as the main swing.

**Capital return:**
- New $1B buyback with no expiry, replacing the $500M programme. Management said it would run "over the next several years," faster if the share price is low.
- Dividend raised 17% to $0.14 a quarter (record date Dec 4).

## The bigger story: Aramark Nexus

Nexus is a new unit, launched April 2026, that feeds and houses workers at remote AI data-center and other large build sites. It is what investors are re-rating the stock on.

- The first hyperscaler site, in Texas, has about 1,000 people on site, ramping toward about 3,500. A second site starts this spring. Together they should pass $150M a year.
- Management targets about $500M of Nexus revenue in fiscal 2027, back-half weighted. UBS models $427M, counting only 4 of 9 announced wins.
- Nexus added about 1 point (about $50M) to Q4 growth.
- **Risks:** management noted regulatory scrutiny of Texas data centers but knows of no delays. The bigger risk is the market's mood on AI. There was an AI-led sell-off on Nov 5 (the S&P 500's worst day since April 2025), and the stock is partly an AI-buildout bet now.

## How the stock got here

- It fell about 12% in the three months to Nov 8, to near $50, sitting just above its 200-day average. It traded at $53.88 before the print.
- A preview called the bar "modest," with bullish sentiment rising.
- Targets: Truist kept Buy at $70 after the print, calling the quarter "solid on an underlying basis." UBS cut to $65 (still Buy) on data-center timing. Consensus is about $68-69, with 14 of 16 analysts at Buy.
- Valuation: about 20x the low end of fiscal 2027 EPS guidance, about $2.70.

## Reading today's price action

Closing up 2.7% after a -4.6% open, on twice normal volume, with the S&P 500 down 1.9%, is a strong reversal on high volume. The market looked past the one-off pay charge and paid for the profit guide, the buyback and the cash flow. There was no follow-through after hours: 55.52, thin trading.

Nearby levels from your screen: the 50-day average at 55.15 is now support, the 20-day high of 56.54 is the first resistance, and the 52-week high is 62.53.

## Risks inside the next 1-10 sessions

- **MLB labour deal:** the contract expires at 10:59 PM CT on Tue Dec 1, and a lockout is widely expected. Owners want a salary cap and the players' union rejects it outright. Aramark's guidance assumes a normal season, and the CEO said they'll "react" if games are lost. A winter lockout costs no games right away, so this is a headline risk only.
- **Market risk:** a falling, AI-sensitive market (AI sell-off, hot inflation, hawkish Fed talk). An AI-trade wobble could hit the Nexus story.
- **Thanksgiving week** brings thin volume.
- The ex-dividend date (about Dec 4) probably falls just outside the window.
- After-hours and broker follow-ups (price-target changes) could come in tonight or tomorrow.

- Sources disagree on some prior-year and expectation figures: last year's Q4 EPS ($0.57 vs $0.64), the retention rate (97% vs about 98%) and fiscal 2026 dollar guidance ($2.27-2.36).
- The company says it met its fiscal 2026 outlook, which was stated as growth rates in constant currency. That fits the actual $2.23, which is below the $2.27-2.36 dollar figure one preview quoted.
- I found no reporting on why the S&P 500 fell on Nov 16.

I've built the story for Tractor Supply (TSCO), the US farm-and-ranch and pet supply retailer. It holds up as a defensive rebound with a modest catalyst behind it, not a turnaround. One limit: the shared web-search budget ran out partway through. The history before July and the Lowe's report date are less checked than the rest.

## Why it rose 4.1% on a bad day for the market
1. **Money moved into safer stocks.** The S&P fell about 1.9%, led by chipmakers (an Nvidia sell-off, plus positioning before Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's expected listing). Only consumer staples and utilities closed higher, and the equal-weight S&P fell only about 1%. TSCO is mostly needs-based (animal feed, pet food, winter supplies), so it trades like a staple on days like this.
2. **Baird note on Monday.** Baird raised its target from $40 to $42, kept Outperform, and named it a "Bullish Fresh Pick" after meeting management in Europe. Only one source (GuruFocus, which I couldn't open) reported this; eToro also lists the $42 raise dated 11/16.
3. **Uber delivery deal, announced Thursday 11/12.** About 2,500 stores are now on Uber, Uber Eats and Postmates, reaching rural and exurban areas, with a $20-off-$60 launch promotion. It's real but small, and was already four days old. One AI-written article named it the "likely" cause, which I'd discount.
4. **Analysts pull both ways.** Evercore downgraded to In Line on Friday 11/13 (target cut from $40 to $38), and Stifel started at Hold ($35) over the weekend. Monday's rise came against that.

## The bigger picture
- **Collapse.** The stock fell from the mid-50s (around $64 at some earlier peak) to about $28 by mid-2026. The causes were a weak pet business (pet comps -4% in Q1), weak big discretionary purchases, a cautious rural consumer and promotions.
- **Low point, Q2 (reported July 23).** Same-store sales fell 1.5%. The company reset 2026 guidance, withdrew its long-term targets from its 2024 investor day (new ones come with Q4 results, about late January), and is closing about 75 Petsense stores (about $75M in charges). Baird cut its target to $38.
- **Q3 (reported Oct 22) beat estimates.** EPS was $0.43 against about $0.41 expected; sales were $3.91B, up 5.1%; same-store sales rose 0.4%. Guidance was reaffirmed, not raised. The stock rose about 4–6% from $32.69.
- **Monthly trend.** Same-store sales were negative in July, modestly positive in August and stronger in September. October ran at the September pace, with the first three and a half weeks of Q4 positive in both customer counts and sales. Management plans for positive Q4 same-store sales.
- **Pressure on profits.** Gross margin fell to 36.4% from 37.4% because of diesel and freight costs and price cuts on about 50 essential items. Operating income fell 10.2%. Q4 gross margin is guided down only 10–30 basis points (vs about 90 in Q3), helped by the new Nampa, Idaho distribution center.
- **Tariff refunds.** About $100M of refunds this year (about $15M of it in Q4) disappear in 2027.
- **Insiders bought.** CEO Hal Lawton bought about $500k of stock, and two directors bought smaller amounts.

agents.report:
On the evidence I found, Monday's 3.6% rise was a reaction to heavy insider buying, set against an open question over whether the dividend gets cut. Two qualifications up front:
- **No same-day headline.** The only item dated today ties the move to the insider purchases. I found no company news and no sector-wide rally for commercial mortgage REITs (companies that lend against commercial property).
- **Search limit hit.** I reached the web search limit before checking the latest analyst notes and how peers traded today. A follow-up message can continue that.

**The business**
- STWD is the largest diversified commercial mortgage REIT, run by Barry Sternlicht.
- Commercial lending is the core: a record $17.8B loan book.
- It also has infrastructure lending, owned property, and LNR, one of the top "special servicers" (firms that manage troubled commercial mortgages for bondholders).
- It is building a roughly $3B net lease business (buildings leased long-term to single tenants).

**Q3 results (Nov 6): the turn in the story**
- **Losses and reserves:** a GAAP loss of $1.08/share, driven by a $337M addition to loan-loss reserves. Total reserves are now about $1.04B, or $2.85/share. The cause was the September rate spike, which made it harder to model borrowers refinancing.
- **Which loans:** the trouble is loans made before 2023, $8.5B or 40% of the book. More than half of the Q3 downgrades were apartment-building loans.
- **Earnings vs. dividend:** distributable earnings (the REIT's dividend-paying measure) were $0.31/share, or $0.41 before realized losses. Both are below the $0.48 quarterly dividend. Management called $0.41 a fair base and said earnings get back toward $0.48 "in a few quarters."
- **Balance sheet:** book value fell to $17.22 from $19.25 at year-end. Leverage rose to 3.1x from 2.4x, and liquidity dropped to $1.1B from $1.4B.
- **Positives:**
  - No new non-accruals (loans that stopped paying) or foreclosures for a second quarter.
  - A Brooklyn office loan returned to paying status.
  - A record $108M of stock was bought back.
  - Special servicing fees rebounded.
- **The dividend:** Sternlicht said "we will have to examine" it. A board meeting is planned and no decision has been made. At Q2, management had said there were no plans to change it.
- **Upside ideas floated:** spinning off the net lease business, or bringing in outside capital, and possible mergers in the sector.
- **Stock reaction:** it slid from $12.88 before earnings to a 52-week low of $11.24, and closed at $11.34 on Nov 13.

**Today's trigger: insider buying**
- Sternlicht bought 830,000 shares at $11.91 on Nov 11 and 415,000 at $11.59 on Nov 12. That is about $14.7M, and it roughly sextupled his direct stake. He said on the call: "I've never sold a share."
- Director Jonathan Pollack bought $1.0M at $11.88 on Nov 11, his first holding.
- The filings came out around Friday Nov 13. Monday opened at $11.75, up from $11.34, and traded as high as about $11.95. It closed at $11.75, exactly where it opened, so the gap held but none of the intraday gain did.
- **Market backdrop:** the S&P fell 1.9% on an Nvidia and chip selloff. The 10-year Treasury yield eased about 4 basis points to roughly 5.12%. Futures priced about a 91% chance of a Fed rate hike in December. Higher rates are this stock's core problem.

**Bull case for 1–10 sessions**
- The CEO bought about $14.7M of stock at $11.59–$11.91, right near today's $11.75, which reads as strong confidence.
- The stock trades at about 0.68x book. Management's math says the price implies roughly 58% losses on the troubled loans and foreclosed property.
- The yield is about 16%, the stock is near its lows, and the 14-day RSI was about 30 on Nov 13 (oversold territory).
- Any drop in rates directly eases the reserve models.

**Bear case**
- The dividend cut is still pending. A reset toward about $0.40 is the base case implied by management's own numbers. A deeper cut or a vague announcement would hit the stock.
- Peers have set the tone: Arbor suspended its dividend on Oct 30.
- With a Fed hike likely, more reserve increases could follow.
- Both the 50-day and 200-day averages are falling, and the 52-week low of $11.24 is only about 4% below.
- Ranges over the last ten sessions are 1.67 times the prior fifty, which means bigger swings in both directions.
- The rise was a one-day news gap that faded from its high. It was not a sector move.

**Timing to watch**
- No date was given for the dividend decision. From memory, not verified this session: STWD usually declares its Q4 dividend in mid-December, which would land just after a ten-session window that ends around Dec 1. A special announcement could come sooner.
- Nvidia reports Tuesday evening and will drive the broad market.
- Any Fed or rates news matters directly here.

agents.report:
RCAT's after-hours drop is an earnings collapse, not a one-off shock. Red Cat reported Q3 after the close today, missed revenue badly and **withdrew its full-year 2026 revenue target**. That removes the main thing that justified the valuation. The market had already priced in part of the bad news, which is why the stock slid into the report.

Note: I ran out of web searches before I could confirm whether Red Cat has an at-the-market share program or new shelf filings, or find any analyst moves dated Tuesday.

## What happened today (Q3 2026, quarter ended September 30)
Source: the company's own release (SEC 8-K exhibit 99.1).
- **Revenue was $11.8M**, up 22% on a year ago. Analysts expected about $40–42M. Revenue for the first nine months is $47.4M.
- **Guidance pulled.** The company had reaffirmed a $150–180M target in August, which needed roughly $100M+ in Q4 alone. Now there is no Q4 or full-year number. Its stated reasons:
  - funding and contract awards are arriving more slowly than expected;
  - its FANG drone was not picked in the Pentagon's Drone Dominance "Gauntlet II" trial.
- **Gross margin was 0.6%** (gross profit $65K), against 16.1% in Q2 and 6.6% a year ago. Management blamed:
  - scrapped FlightWave inventory;
  - warranty costs and higher returns;
  - factory capacity sitting idle.
- **Losses widened.** Operating loss was $43.4M, net loss $40.4M (−$0.26 a share, about 5 cents worse than expected), and adjusted EBITDA −$37.5M. Operating expenses rose to $43.5M from $18.2M; R&D rose to $16.1M from $6.0M.
- **Cash fell to $242.7M** from $325.6M at the end of June. Operations used $156.8M in the first nine months, mostly to build inventory. Inventory is now $117–127M (the release's figures don't reconcile), up from $23.5M at the end of 2025. Management says it is not perishable and needs no write-down reserve, but this quarter included a scrap charge.
- **Positives management offered on the call:**
  - Blue Ops (its drone-boat unit) got a first US government order, for two B-26 boats.
  - Black Widow drone work with the US Air Force has restarted.

## PG&E (PCG): the story as of Monday night, 2026-11-16

**In short:** PG&E is a California utility whose stock is priced almost entirely on one political question: will California limit what utilities owe when their equipment starts a wildfire? The stock fell about 20% in one day on August 31 when the Legislature dropped that relief. Since then it has traded in a narrow $12 to $14 band while the company lobbies for a fix and threatens to restructure. I found no company- or policy-specific news that explains today's +3.2% gain on a day the S&P fell 1.9%. My web search limit ran out before I could finish the last few checks (listed at the end).

### 1. How it got here
- **Liability rule.** Under California's inverse-condemnation doctrine, a utility pays for fire damage its equipment causes even if it wasn't negligent. Insurers then sue the utility to recover what they paid out to homeowners, which is called subrogation. These liabilities pushed PG&E into bankruptcy in 2019, and the January 2025 Eaton fire (caused by Southern California Edison) threatens to drain the state's $21B wildfire fund. PG&E has the largest exposure of the three big California utilities.
- **August 31, 2026: down about 20%, its largest daily move.** The Legislature passed a narrowed SB 492 without the protections Governor Newsom had sought: a per-fire cap on withdrawals from the fund, a ban on subrogation suits, and a way to refill the fund. PG&E went from about $18 to about $13.40. BMO, Wells Fargo, Mizuho and Bank of America downgraded it.
- **September 1: up about 6% to $14.06.** The Assembly let even the narrowed bill die without a vote. Newsom said the state must "return to fix the entire problem." The Assembly promised hearings later in the year. KCRA cited a source saying activist investors had contacted PG&E's board.
- **Q3 results, October 22.** Core EPS guidance was reaffirmed: $1.64–1.66 for 2026 and $1.78–1.82 for 2027. On the negative side:
  - PG&E cut $2B from its 2027 capital plan, citing financing costs.
  - Fitch moved its outlook to negative.
  - The company is still rated below investment grade.
  - It launched a strategic review aimed at creating one or more investment-grade businesses. Options include a regulator-approved spin, sale or separation of the gas business, plus "everything on the table," including the dividend.
  - The CEO said reform is the fastest way to unlock value and that issuing equity at this price is "not an option." The CFO said no new equity is needed through 2030.
  - The review's outcome is reportedly due by summer 2027.
- **Late October to early November: the lobbying push.**
  - October 29: a joint Assembly hearing on subrogation.
  - November 1: a CPUC report prepared at Newsom's request. The PUC's director warned that uncapped liability risks credit downgrades.
  - November 3, per the LA Times: the utilities asked for a permanent cap on shareholder liability, even when the utility was imprudent, at about one-fifth of transmission and distribution equity rate base. That is about $5.1B for PG&E, with costs above the cap passed to customers. They wanted it passed in a special session before Thanksgiving.
  - Edison's CEO said the current legislature ends November 30 and a special-session bill had to be sent by November 15. **That date has now passed, and I found no sign that a session was called.** Insiders described rank-and-file legislators as cold to the idea.
  - PG&E is also delaying some new grid hookups until the issue is settled. Critics call that "bailout blackmail."
- **New political risk.** Governor-elect Becerra takes office in January. He says liability reform is a priority but has given no details and voiced concern for insurers. He has also proposed freezing utility bills and home insurance premiums. PG&E spent more than $13M against his rival in the primary. Regulators would have to approve any rate freeze, and the CPUC president has questioned how it would work.

### 2. Today's move
- I found no PG&E-specific news for November 13 or 16. The latest company release was the November 9 milestone of 1,500 miles of buried power lines.
- A market recap that matches today's –1.9% S&P drop says only consumer staples (+0.3%) and utilities (+0.1%) rose. So defensive rotation explains a little of the move, but PCG beat its own sector by about 3 points.
- Friday also rose 2.2%, to $13.25, so this is two strong days in a row.
- The most likely unconfirmed drivers are renewed hope of a December or early-January deal (the new legislature meets in December) or chatter about the strategic review or activists. I could not verify either.
- A trust connected to an insider sold shares at $13.22 on November 13 (Form 4). It is small and probably minor.

### 3. Setup and what matters over the next 1–10 sessions
- **Price.** The stock has been stuck between roughly $12 and $14 since August 31. Today's close of $13.68 sits at the top of that range, just under the 20-day high of $13.73 and the September 1 rebound close of $14.06. A close above about $14.06 would be the first break out of the post-crash range. The 200-day average of $16.04 marks roughly the level before the August crash.
- **Upside triggers** (these would be big gaps, not drift): a special session being called, a deal outline from Newsom or Becerra, or the strategic review producing something concrete such as a gas spin or an activist stake.
- **Downside risks:**
  - A Becerra rate-freeze push.
  - More criticism of the hookup delays.
  - A cut to the CPUC undergrounding plan, or the final 2027 rate case decision. A proposed decision would allow $456M of interim recovery starting in January.
  - A credit rating downgrade.
  - Any reported failure of the reform push now that the November 15 date has passed.
- **Fire risk** is seasonally lower now that the rainy season has started, which makes a new ignition shock less likely in this window.
- **Analysts.** Average price target is about $17.6–22, depending on the source; Google Finance counts 5 Buy and 7 Hold. I found no rating changes in November.
- **Overall.** The story is a binary policy bet. Absent news, quiet trading (ranges at 0.65× the prior fifty sessions) near the top of the range is consistent with drift. The headline risk runs both ways and can gap the stock hard: –20% and +6% within two days in late August.

Tyson also said many Americans are trying to eat more protein and that its packaged foods unit gained market share. That reads across to Hormel, though no source links the two moves directly. The fine print was weaker: Tyson guided 2027 chicken profit down to $1.3–1.6B because of more industry supply and higher grain costs.
- **Volume was ordinary.** HRL traded about 6.03M shares today. It traded more on Oct 30 (11.1M) and Nov 2 (6.6M), so today does not look like a big buyer arriving.

- The deal was announced Sep 30 and was expected to close in Hormel's fiscal first quarter, so closing now is roughly on time, not a surprise.
- Hormel expects the deal to add to adjusted earnings per share only from fiscal 2028, with about $20M a year in cost savings. It roughly triples Hormel's chicken business.
- Hormel said it will give more detail on the deal and its fiscal 2027 outlook on the Dec 3 earnings call. The +2.1% after hours is most likely this news on thin trading.

Management now sees about $0.37 for the fourth quarter at the midpoint, with $0.40 at the top. The stock fell about 9% after that report.

I found a clear story, though it isn't a single news event. The three are being sold together on a squeeze on lower-income shoppers and on fears ahead of their earnings reports. Underneath that is one specific fight: Ross is taking customers from TJX's biggest chain. Both TJX and Ross report inside the next one to ten sessions, so this is a bet on earnings, not a slow drift. My web search budget ran out before I could look into Ross and Burlington's October moves, so a few gaps are listed at the end.

**1. Pressure on the whole group (weeks to months)**
- **The core shopper is squeezed.** October producer prices rose 6.5% from a year ago, the most since late 2022, and goods prices rose 10.2%. The 10-year Treasury yield is about 5.12%. The market puts about a 91% chance on a Fed rate *hike* at the December 9 meeting. Consumer sentiment is around 51. Analysts are worried that higher rates and prices hit lower-income shoppers, who are central to off-price and dollar stores.
- **Freight costs.** Fighting with Iran and incidents in the Strait of Hormuz have kept oil high (Brent about $96). Diesel was about $6.35 a gallon in October, near its record. Bank of America (Lorraine Hutchinson) cut her earnings estimates and price targets on all three over freight costs but kept Buy ratings. Back in March, Bank of America had argued these chains absorb freight costs better than most because they sell pricier items per unit shipped.
- **Earnings are flattered by one-off money.** All three booked refunds of tariffs collected under emergency powers (TJX $219M, Ross about $253M or about $0.60 a share, Burlington $55M). That inflates this year's earnings per share and makes next year's comparison harder.

**2. TJX: TJ Maxx and Marshalls are losing shoppers to Ross**
- **August report (Q2):** TJX beat estimates, but its biggest division, Marmaxx (TJ Maxx and Marshalls), grew same-store sales only 1%. All of that came from bigger baskets; the number of transactions fell slightly. Management blamed its own merchandise choices and execution. Its Q3 forecast came in below estimates. The stock fell 6.7% that day and another 9.3% over the next five days. It was $170 at the June peak; the 52-week low is about $122.78 to $125.49.
- **Friday, Nov 13:** Gordon Haskett cut TJX to Hold with a $130 target, saying Wall Street is "far too complacent" about competition. Its foot-traffic data at stores near each other still favours Ross over Marmaxx. Wells Fargo cut its target from $140 to $135 (Equal Weight). Jim Cramer's charity trust sold about half its TJX stake to limit the risk if Marmaxx disappoints again.
- **Today, Nov 16:** Morgan Stanley cut its target from $178 to $166 but kept Overweight. Earlier, UBS cut from $198 to $184 and Bank of America to $170, and Cantor started coverage at Neutral with $139. The average target is about $167 to $170, against today's close of about $131.09.
- **Options and valuation (as of Nov 15):** The put/call ratio was 0.96 against a 20-day average of 0.82, a defensive tilt. Short interest is low at 1.5%. The P/E is about 23.9.
- **What the report needs:** the company forecast Q3 same-store sales up 2% to 3%. Consensus is $1.33 a share on $15.81B of sales. TJX has beaten earnings estimates eight quarters running, yet fell after the last report. The Marmaxx number decides the reaction, not the headline result.

**3. Ross: the winner, with a high bar**
- **August report (Q2):** same-store sales rose 10%, driven by more shoppers, and total sales rose 13%. It raised its full-year outlook.
- **Q3 forecast:** same-store sales up 6% to 7% and earnings of $1.75 to $1.83 a share. Consensus is about $1.82, near the top of that range.
- **The bar is higher still.** Deutsche Bank (Krisztina Katai) raised its Ross same-store estimate to 9% from 7%. It names Ross and TJX its preferred off-price stocks into 2027.
- **The stock is still falling.** Ross fell about 2.3% on Friday and 3.8% today, and Wells Fargo cut its target (Equal Weight). Even the share winner is being sold. That looks like de-risking ahead of the report, not a change in the story. The risk is that a beat which merely meets a whisper of about 9% doesn't lift the stock.

**4. Burlington: the weakest of the three on business trends**
- **August report (Q2):** same-store sales rose only 2%, and sales of $2.99B missed estimates. New stores took sales from existing ones, cutting same-store growth by about 1.5 points.
- **Forecast:** same-store sales up 1% to 3% for both Q3 and Q4.
- **Estimates cut:** Deutsche Bank cut its Burlington same-store estimate to 2% from 4%, citing weather and softer trends.
- **Stock:** Burlington fell 3.6% on Friday. It reports around Nov 24 or 25 before the open (sources differ), so it trades on the read-across from TJX and Ross first.

**5. Today in context**
- **The whole market fell.** The S&P 500 fell 1.92%, led by tech (Nvidia's leadership turmoil, new chip export curbs). Consumer discretionary fell 1.53%, and only staples and utilities rose. Volatility (VIX) jumped 18.7% to 22.9.
- **The group still lagged retail.** The basket's extra 1.5% drop against XRT (the retail ETF) is in line with money moving from discretionary into staples before these reports.
- **What I couldn't explain:** I found no single event behind the 12% underperformance against XRT over 20 days. TJX was about $138 on Oct 28 and about $131 now, so some of the gap may be XRT holding up rather than a collapse in the basket.

**Dated catalysts (Central time)**
- **Tue Nov 17, 7:30 AM CT:** October retail sales (forecast +0.6%, prior +0.8%). The question is whether shoppers are buying more items or just paying higher prices.
- **Wed Nov 18, before the open:** TJX Q3. Lowe's and Target report the same morning.
- **Thu Nov 19, 3:00 PM CT:** Ross Q3 after the close; the call is at 3:15 PM CT. The Trump–Xi meeting at APEC, where tariff cuts are being discussed, is due the same day.
- **About Nov 24 or 25, before the open:** Burlington Q3.
- **Dec 9:** Fed decision, with a hike expected.

**How to read it for a one-to-ten-session trade**
- **The bear case:** a squeezed core shopper, freight costs set to hit margins when trucking contracts renew in April, Marmaxx losing share, Burlington's same-store sales slowing, and earnings flattered by refunds.
- **The bull case:** bargain-hunting holiday shoppers. The stocks are washed out (TJX is about 23% below its high, below its 20-day low, with defensive options positioning). Most analysts keep Buy ratings with targets well above the price, and TJX has beaten for eight straight quarters.
- **Treat it as two separate earnings bets.** A swing trade entered now holds through both reports.
  - TJX trades on whether Marmaxx transactions turn back up.
  - Ross trades on beating a whisper of about 9% same-store sales.
- **Burlington moves on what the other two say.**
- **Watch the TJX vs Ross split.** If Marmaxx improves, the Gordon Haskett share-loss thesis weakens and TJX probably outperforms Ross. If Marmaxx stays weak, Ross probably holds up better than TJX.

**Gaps:** I couldn't confirm the size of the Bank of America target cuts, a TJX earnings forecast for Q3 (the 2% to 3% same-store forecast is confirmed), any Burlington analyst moves this month, or why Ross and Burlington fell in October. Some sources gave conflicting prices and dates; I used the dated, consistent ones. A follow-up can cover those once searches are available again.

**Bottom line:** Tonight's +6.8% is a reaction to earnings, and the news is real but modest. AECOM's fiscal Q4 beat on profit, its fiscal 2027 guidance came in at or slightly above what analysts expected, and the troubled construction project is on track. That lands on a stock that had already rebounded about 25% from its October low. The stock is still cheap against its peers (about 12x guided earnings versus about 20x for Jacobs). But the story now hinges on Tuesday's 7:00 AM CT conference call, and on whether the market treats this as a turning point or as a stretched rally that has been confirmed and should be sold.

### How it fell from about $133 to $56 over the past year
1. **Nov 18, 2025:** AECOM reported fiscal 2025 results. It raised its long-term targets (margin above 20% by FY28, adjusted EPS growth above 15% a year, organic net service revenue growth of 5-8%) and put its Construction Management (CM) business up for possible sale. The stock still fell about 11%. Baird downgraded AECOM and Jacobs to Neutral, citing uncertainty about AI.
2. **Feb 2026:** AECOM decided to keep CM rather than sell it. On Feb 12, fear that AI would cut billable engineering hours hit the whole sector, and ACM was the worst performer at about -12% (Jacobs about -8%). By March it was near $60, down about 30% in six months.
3. **Aug 10, 2026 (fiscal Q3):** A $337M pre-tax charge on a CM project won in 2019 under terms that would fail today's risk rules. That gave an adjusted loss of -$0.50 against roughly +$1.51 expected. Fiscal 2026 EPS guidance was cut to $3.95-4.15 (about $6.00 excluding the charge), and the stock fell about 9-10%. The 52-week low of $56.10 came in this period.
4. **Mid-October to now:** The stock climbed from about $58 to $72.50. I found no single trigger. Contributors were a Zacks upgrade to Hold on Oct 28, a Jacobs/AECOM joint-venture win on an Irish Rail consultancy framework (Nov 13), a cheap valuation, and positioning ahead of earnings. - **Q4 results:** Adjusted EPS was $1.63, up 20%, against $1.59 expected. Adjusted EBITDA was $358M against about $352M expected. Revenue missed at $3.88B against about $4.0-4.1B expected, down 7%. Segment margin was a record 18.2% (up 110 basis points), helped by International at a record 14.8%.
- **Backlog and wins:** Backlog hit a record $28.0B, up 13%, and International backlog rose 21%. Wins for the year were a record $13.4B, 1.3x what it billed (Q4 alone: 1.1x). The Middle East returned to growth.

  - Adjusted EPS of $6.15-6.35. The $6.25 midpoint is roughly in line with consensus; sources put consensus at $6.06, $6.23 or $6.24.

I found no single news item that explains today's move. It looks like a defensive rotation: money left AI and tech, and the payroll and HR names are seen as the low-beta part of software that gains when hiring is strong and interest rates are high. Most of the 3.7% edge probably came from IGV falling, not from the basket rising.

**1. What happened today (Mon 11/16)**
- The S&P 500 fell 1.92% to 7,416.59, its third straight loss. The Nasdaq fell 2.49% and the Nasdaq-100 2.67%. The VIX rose 18.7% to 22.9.
- The cause was the AI trade:
  - Nvidia fell 4.1% after reports its board is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang. Its earnings come Tuesday after the close.
  - Commerce tightened AI chip export rules.
  - Investors are positioning ahead of Anthropic's IPO: 825M shares at $70–78, pricing Wednesday, trading Thursday as "ANT", reportedly about 7x oversubscribed.
- Technology was the worst sector at -3.24%. Only Consumer Staples and Utilities finished higher, and decliners beat gainers 355 to 145. The equal-weight S&P fell only 1.01%.
- Software was mixed: HubSpot +6.8%, BILL +5.8% (William Blair upgrade), Qualys +5.2%, DigitalOcean -8.6%.
- Two daily recaps named none of the five payroll stocks.
- What this means for the signal: IGV likely fell about 3% today. With PCTY the best name at +3.5% and WDAY the worst at -1.2%, the basket's own move was probably only slightly positive.
- The only name-specific item: PCTY hit a 52-week high of about $181.61–182.34 intraday. Its prior close was $178.22.

**2. The bigger story over the last 20 days: four supports**
- **Strong hiring.** October payrolls rose 165k, roughly double expectations. Unemployment fell to 4.1%, and August and September were revised up by 84k. Today's Empire State employment index was the highest since June 2022. Payroll firms are paid per employee processed, so hiring growth lifts revenue directly.
- **High interest rates.** The 10-year is around 4.9–5.15%; sources disagree, and today's recaps give 5.12% and 5.15%. December hike odds are about 75–81%, with the FOMC meeting December 8–9. Payroll processors earn interest on client funds they hold before paying them out. That reasoning is my own general knowledge; no 2026 source I found confirmed it. Higher rates hurt long-duration growth software but help this group.
- **Clean earnings with buybacks.** Every name except WDAY has reported, and all beat:
  - **ADP (10/28):** revenue +6%, adjusted EPS +13% to $2.82 against $2.77 expected, guidance raised. The stock dipped about 2.5% on the day.
  - **ADP dividend (11/11):** raised 12% to $7.60 a year, the 52nd straight annual increase. ADP was about $309 on 11/13.
  - **PAYC (11/4):** revenue $543.8M (+10%), adjusted EPS $3.37 against $2.81 expected, full-year guidance raised to $2.213–2.218B. BTIG then downgraded it Buy→Neutral on 11/5, and it had come back to about $249 by 11/13 from about $268 after earnings. It is up roughly 105% in six months, helped by buybacks of about $1.4B in the first half that cut the share count about 20%.
  - **PCTY (11/5):** revenue $451.7M (+10.7%), recurring revenue +12%, $152.5M of buybacks. Full-year revenue guidance is $1.910–1.925B, but it implies only about 9% recurring growth, a slowdown. BTIG ($210) and Citi ($214) raised targets. The consensus target of about $178 is now below the price, and insiders sold about $26.5M over 90 days.
  - **PAYX (9/23, quarter to August):** revenue +6%, guidance kept at 5–6%, PEO guidance raised to 7–8%. Dividend is $1.19 a quarter, about 10% higher than a year ago. The stock was about $116 on 11/10–11/13, well below its old highs. Its 52-week low is $85.45, and sources disagree on the high.
- **Seen as surviving AI.** The February 2026 software selloff, which wiped out nearly $1T and was triggered by Anthropic's automation tools, hit seat-based software hardest. Payroll and compliance work is regulated, involves moving money and has high switching costs, so investors have been treating it as relatively safe. Tech fell about 12% in October while WDAY rose about 6%. Much of the basket's 12.2% gain against IGV is IGV falling.

**3. Workday is the odd one out**
- In August, Reuters reported Silver Lake was in talks to take Workday private, valuing it around $51B. The stock had its best day in a decade, closing at $206.45.
- No deal has been announced. I found no update after August.
- WDAY was about $196 on 11/13, down about 8.5% year to date. Its 52-week range is $110–237.
- It reports fiscal Q3 on **Tuesday 11/24 at 3:30 PM CT**, six sessions from now. Consensus is EPS $2.74 on revenue of $2.69B. It trades at about 17.8x forward earnings.
- It is the most AI-exposed name in the basket (seat-based enterprise HR), which fits it being the worst today at -1.2%.

**4. What could move the group in the next 1–10 sessions**
- **Tue 11/17:** retail sales (forecast +0.6%); Nvidia earnings after the close.
- **Wed–Thu 11/18–19:** Anthropic prices and starts trading. This is a two-way risk:
  - A strong debut could pull money back into AI and high-beta tech, and the defensive trade could unwind against IGV.
  - Any "AI agents replace software" framing could also hit software broadly. The February selloff began with Anthropic news.
- **Tue 11/24:** Workday earnings, with any word on Silver Lake. This is the biggest single-name risk in the basket.
- **11/26–27:** Thanksgiving, with markets closed on the 26th and a half day on the 27th. Liquidity will be thin.
- **Just past the window:** ADP's private jobs report (around 12/2), November payrolls (12/4) and the FOMC (12/8–9). All of these work as catalysts for this group.

**5. How I read it**
- **Bull case:** Strong hiring, high rates and clean earnings with buybacks give the group a real reason to outperform. The move has been building for 20 days and is not a one-day spike.
- **Bear case:**
  - The edge against IGV mostly comes from IGV falling, so it is a bet on AI and tech staying weak.
  - Valuations are stretched: PAYC is up about 105% in six months and was downgraded, and PCTY trades above its consensus target with insiders selling.
  - Workday earnings and the Anthropic debut both land inside the hold window.
